items.stem: Define the term 'negligence'.
items.answer: A tort where the defendant owes the claimant a duty of care, breaches that duty and causes the claimant damage that is not too remote.

items.stem: Zara ran a gym where an unsecured weight fell on Amara, a member. Amara was injured as a result. Amara wants to sue Zara in negligence. Advise Amara whether Zara owed Amara a duty of care. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: established duties are applied by precedent (Robinson v CC West Yorkshire 2018); novel cases: Caparo test of foreseeability, proximity and fair, just and reasonable, developed incrementally; neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson); no general duty to prevent harm by third parties (Hill; Michael). Application: Zara ran a gym where an unsecured weight fell on Amara, a member; this is an established or analogous duty to visitors and customers. Conclusion: This is an established or analogous duty to visitors and customers.

items.stem: Priya, an employee of Mei Ltd, was injured at work in Madrid when a guard rail that Mei Ltd had failed to repair gave way. Priya had a rare bone condition, so the injury was far more serious than expected. Advise Priya on whether Mei Ltd is liable for all of the harm suffered. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: but for test (Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington HMC); intervening acts may break the chain (Knightley v Johns; McKew v Holland); remoteness: reasonably foreseeable type of damage (The Wagon Mound No 1); manner need not be foreseen (Hughes); thin skull rule (Smith v Leech Brain). Application: but for Mei Ltd's breach, Priya would not have been injured; Priya had a rare bone condition, so the injury was far more serious than expected.; so the thin skull rule makes Mei Ltd liable for the full extent (Smith v Leech Brain). Conclusion: Mei Ltd is liable for the original injury; for the later harm, the thin skull rule makes Mei Ltd liable for the full extent (Smith v Leech Brain).

items.stem: Contractors working for Diego Ltd negligently cut a power cable outside Jonas Ltd's bakery in Lisbon. The power was off for 24 hours. Jonas Ltd lost stock worth $15 000 that spoiled and also lost profits of $50 000 because production stopped. Advise Jonas Ltd on what loss it can recover.
items.answer: Law: physical damage and consequential economic loss are recoverable; pure economic loss is generally not recoverable (Spartan Steel v Martin; Murphy v Brentwood). Application: the stock worth $15 000 that spoiled is physical damage and recoverable, with any profit directly on it; the lost profits of $50 000 from stopped production are pure economic loss. Conclusion: Jonas Ltd can recover for the damaged stock and consequential loss, but not the $50 000 of pure economic loss.

items.answer: Law: a recognised psychiatric illness is required; primary victims in the zone of danger recover if physical injury was foreseeable (Page v Smith); secondary victims must satisfy Alcock: close tie, proximity in time and space or immediate aftermath (McLoughlin), own unaided senses; rescuers must be in danger (White v CC South Yorkshire; Chadwick). Application: PTSD is a recognised psychiatric illness; Yusuf watched the event live on television at home, knowing Yusuf's brother was at the festival; so Yusuf is a secondary victim who fails Alcock because there was no perception with own unaided senses and the tie must be proved. Conclusion: Yusuf is a secondary victim who fails Alcock because there was no perception with own unaided senses and the tie must be proved.

Application: PTSD is a recognised psychiatric illness; Zara arrived at hospital two hours later and saw Zara's own spouse there, badly injured and not yet treated,; so Zara is a secondary victim within the immediate aftermath (McLoughlin v O'Brian). Conclusion: Zara is a secondary victim within the immediate aftermath (McLoughlin v O'Brian).
